background.definition: Failure of the neural tube to close during the fourth week of embryogenesis results in the protrusion of the spinal cord and/or meninges through a defective vertebral arch, leading to a subcutaneous fatty mass, a cystic lesion, or an open defect. The terms meningomyelocele and myelomeningocele are generally used interchangeably.

list.listitem: 1 of every 900 to 1000 live births have myelomeningocele.
2000 new patients every year in the United States.
1 in 4000 live births have spinal lipomas.
Learning disabilities and cognitive impairment correlate highly with myelomeningocele necessitating educational interventions and speech therapy.
Motor disabilities result in need for occupational and physical therapy as well as assistive devices such as wheelchair, braces, and walkers.
Patients with myelomeningocele are 1 to 2 standard deviation units below normal for bone mineral density increasing the risk of pathologic fractures.
Women with meningomyelocele may have altered sexual functioning, especially if they experience urinary incontinence.
There are multiple genetic syndromes associated with myelomeningocele including Vater syndrome, Knobloch syndrome, Trisomy 13, and Klippel-Feil syndrome.

Genes associated with myelomeningocele include PRICKLE2, GLI3, RAB23, HES1, FOLR1. In one study of cell-free RNA in amniotic fluid of 10 women carrying fetuses with open myelomeningocele, novel dysregulated genes were identified in association with neurodevelopment and neuronal regeneration (up-regulated, GAP43 and ZEB1) or axonal growth and guidance (down-regulated, ACAP1).
Most of the nonsyndromic neural tube defects (NTDs) are multifactorial in origin.
Dietary folate deficiency increases the risk of NTDs.
There is an association between NTDs and increasing maternal obesity as well as prenatal maternal exposure to valproic acid or rubella, and maternal hyperthermia in early gestation.
It is likely formed from premature detachment of the neural tube from the cutaneous ectoderm causing the folding neuroectoderm to maintain its cleft dorsally.
The vertebral bodies are missing posterior elements at different affected levels and there is extension of the subarachnoid space posteriorly through the bony spina bifida thus creating the defect.

Risk_Factor.Risk_Name: Maternal exposure to valproic acid or carbamazepine
Family history of neural tube defects or other "schisis" disorders
Intrauterine hyperthermia from both maternal illness or hot tub use during first months of pregnancy

list.listitem: Offer material alpha fetoprotein screening for NTDs to all pregnant women, and order ultrasound if the test result is abnormal to look for neural tube defects. B

All persons who plan to or could become pregnant should take 0.4 to 0.8 mg of folic acid supplementation daily, A and high-risk women, such as those with a prior history of NTDs, should take 4 mg daily to prevent NTDs. B
Offer material alpha fetoprotein screening for NTDs to all pregnant women, and order ultrasound if the test result is abnormal to look for neural tube defects.

The Canadian 2021 guideline recommends first-trimester (12 to 14 weeks gestation) and routine second-trimester (18 to 22 weeks gestation) sonographic examination for screening and diagnosis of fetal NTDs as first-line screening, with material alpha fetoprotein screening used as a primary screening tool for limited clinical indications (e.g., if geographical location or clinical factors such as obesity limit timely and high-quality sonographic screening at 18 to 22 weeks). They also recommend use of second-trimester maternal alpha fetoprotein for secondary screening as a complement to maternal serum cell-free placental DNA aneuploidy screening.

Using a ratio between brain stem diameter and its distance to the occipital bone obtained during first trimester ultrasound, investigators found a pooled sensitivity of 0.70 (95% CI 0.47-0.87; I2 = 78.3%), specificity of 1.00 (95% CI 0.99-1.0; I2 = 99.2%), LR + of 51.44 (95% CI 9.53-277.64; I2 = 85.5%), LR- of 0.23 (95% CI 0.04-1.17; I2 = 64.8%), and an AUC of 0.9649 for detecting open spina bifida.
Failure of newborn hearing screening appears to be more common in infants with meningomyelocele and is associated with subsequent brainstem symptoms.

The USPSTF 2023 recommends that all persons who plan to or could become pregnant take 0.4 to 0.8 mg of folic acid supplementation daily; the critical period for protection against NTDs being 1 month before to the first 2-3 months of pregnancy. Higher dose folic acid supplementation at 4 mg/d is recommended for women at high risk for NTD including having given birth to a child with an NTD. The Canadian 2021 guideline recommends supplementation with a daily multivitamin containing 1.0 mg folic acid and vitamin B12 for women at moderate risk and emphasizes that supplementation should begin at least 3 months before conception for those at moderate or high risk.

Authors of a Cochrane review of 5 trials found hig- quality evidence that daily folic acid supplementation alone or in combination with other vitamins and minerals is effective in preventing NTDs compared with no interventions/placebo or vitamins and minerals without folic acid (RR 0.31; 95% CI 0.17-0.58). Provision of folic acid does not appear to prevent all NTDs or other types of birth defects such as cleft palate/lip or cardiovascular defects.

Authors of a systematic review of 24 studies found consistent evidence from pre-fortification studies of a protective effect for NTD, including the single RCT, with OR ranging from 0.11 to 0.7, but no benefit from more recent case-control studies.
Folic acid has a significant protective effect for recurrence (RR 0.34; 95% CI 0.18-0.64) based on four studies and 1846 births.
A folate-containing oral contraceptive (Beyaz®) is available that may help reduce the risk of NTDs in a pregnancy conceived during use or shortly after discontinuation of the product.
Follow bone mineral density in patients with myelomeningocele as they are at risk for pathologic bone fractures.
Ninety-five percent of myelomeningocele are diagnosed prenatally with the combination of ultrasound and AFP on maternal serum. B
Fetal MRI is a useful adjunct when sonography data are nondiagnostic. C
Assess patients for associated facial malformations, renal anomalies, and congenital heart defects. C

Spina bifida occulta, meningocele, myelomeningocele, myelocystocele, myeloschisis

list.listitem: Depending on the level of the lesion at which the spinal cord is interrupted, symptoms can manifest as paralysis of the legs, fecal and urinary incontinence, abnormalities of the hips, knees, and feet, and sensory deficits of the skin in affected regions. Children with myelomeningocele may have associated hydrocephalus, Arnold–Chiari malformation (structural defects in the cerebellum), or progressive scoliosis.
Newborns with myelomeningocele do not appear to have high levels of pain or discomfort as measured by a visual analog scale for pain and the Comfort Behavioral Scale.

Be vigilant for increasing head circumference, vomiting, seizures, or a bulging fontanelle to identify advancing hydrocephalus in neonates and infants. A midline sinus tract, tuft of hair, or a SC lipoma can also signal underlying spinal pathology. In one case series of 56 children with hair collar sign (scalp alopecia surrounded by a ring of hypertrichosis) or hair tuft of the scalp who underwent cranial and brain imaging, 23 (41%) had abnormal findings including cranial/bone defect (30.4%), defect with direct communication with the central nervous system (28.6%); venous malformations (25%); or central nervous system abnormalities (12.5%).
See complications
Most infants are diagnosed prenatally with prenatal genetic screening or ultrasound. The diagnosis is apparent on physical exam postnatally and confirmed wtih imaging.

Order a cranial ultrasound to detect early signs of hydrocephalus in infants with spina bifida. It offers the advantage of low cost, good visualization, and no radiation exposure. Ventricular dilatation is the most sensitive sign of hydrocephalus.
Consider MRI of brain and spine to evaluate for hydrocephalus, Chiari malformations and spinal cord dysraphism (neurologic disorders related to spinal malformation, including spinal cord tethering).

Prenatal ultrasound was able to determined the correct level of the lesion 41% of the time, and was within 1 level 76% of the time. Fetal MRI had similar accuracy. Order fetal MRI when ultrasound is nondiagnostic.
CT scan of the brain and spine are used to assess for abnormalities of the vertebrae, evolving hydrocephalus, and shunt malfunction.

For cases in which a diagnostic amniocentesis has been performed, the Canadian 2021 guideline recommends that the amniotic fluid specimen be evaluated for fetal genetic abnormalities. This evaluation should consist of chromosomal microarray and other genetic testing, as considered appropriate after assessment of fetal anomalies and family history, with amniotic fluid alpha fetoprotein and amniotic fluid acetylcholinesterase, if required by protocols for fetal surgery decisions.
Renal ultrasound, renal nucleotide scans, and voiding cystourethrograms are recommended to follow the patients for kidney reflux, parenchymal renal damage, and outlet obstruction.

For children with spina bifida on clean intermittent catheterization, leukocyte esterase testing (LET) vs. lab culture can be used to exclude significant bacteriuria at home. In one study of 112 children, a negative LET excluded significant bacteriuria (negative predictive value 96%) while a positive LET had a positive predictive value of 72%.

Clinicians should discuss options with families following identification of a pregnancy with a fetus with an NTD. These include: prenatal surgical repair of myelomeningocele, including prognosis; post-natal surgical repair of myelomeningocele, including prognosis; and pregnancy termination with autopsy.
See for a suggested approach to management of the patient with an NTD.
Delivery should be conducted at a facility capable of managing all aspects of high-risk neonatal delivery. No specific delivery route provides a more beneficial outcome. B

If significant hydrocephalus is present, perform shunt placement via VP shunt or endoscopic third ventricle ventriculostomy and provide close follow-up for development or progression of hydrocephalus. B
Early surgical in utero intervention of the normal karyotype newborn can improve social, cognitive, and medical outcomes. B
Treatment should be coordinated by a multidisciplinary team (). C
Prescribe anticonvulsants for underlying seizure disorder.

Prophylactic antibiotics are used in some patients with spina bifida who are on clean intermittent catheterization to reduce the incidence of urinary tract infection (UTI). In one study of 176 patients, discontinuation of low dose chemoprophylaxis resulted in higher rates of UTI (RR 1.44; 95% CI 1.13-1.83) which translates into 1 extra UTI each year for every 2 patients discontinuing antibiotics. Of 88 patients allocated to discontinuation, just under half (43%) switched back to chemoprophylaxis at the end of the study.
Primary back closure of the open NTD in early infancy should occur, if not discovered during pregnancy. Surgical repair of closed defects can be delayed for several months.

The 2019 Congress of Neurological Surgeons guidelines concluded, based on a systematic review, that evidence is insufficient to determine if closure within 48 hours after birth reduces the risk of infection. They further recommend that if closure is delayed beyond 48 hours that antibiotics be given.

ACOG (2017) recommends that women carrying a fetus with myelomeningocele who meet established criteria for in-utero repair (e.g., defect at T1 through S1 with hindbrain herniation; gestational age at surgery no greater than 25 weeks, 6 days; maternal age 18 years or higher; singleton pregnancy) should be counseled in a nondirective fashion with surgery offered only to carefully selected patients at facilities with an appropriate level of personnel and resources.

Fetal surgery results in improved outcomes. Practice criteria have been published by the Maternal-Fetal Management Task Force convened by the Eunice Kennedy Shriver National Institute of Child Health and Human Development. In an RCT of 183 infants, prenatal surgery before 26 weeks of gestation was found to be superior to standard postnatal repair for myelomeningocele; the trial was stopped early when the primary outcome of a composite of fetal or neonatal death or the need for shunt placement by age 12 months was reached in 68% of the infants in the prenatal-surgery group and in 98% of those in the postnatal-surgery group. Prenatal surgery, however, was associated with an increased risk of preterm delivery, and uterine dehiscence at delivery.
Fetal surgery was also shown to improve future gastrointestinal outcomes.
For follow-up information for children in the above RCT, see Prognosis.
Prenatal surgery is also endorsed by 2019 Congress of Neurological Surgeons guidelines as preferable when possible as it leads to better early outcomes. The impact on late outcomes are uncertain.

Earlier gestational age at surgery and chorioamniotic membrane separation were associated with increased risk of spontaneous membrane rupture (odds ratio [OR] 1.49; 95% confidence interval [CI] 1.01-2.22; and OR 2.96; 95% CI 1.05-8.35, respectively), and oligohydramnios was associated with an increased risk of subsequent preterm delivery (OR 9.21; 95% CI 2.19-38.78).

Authors of a Cochrane review found only the above well-conducted trial of prenatal vs. postnatal repair for 158 infants with open spina bifida making it difficult to draw conclusions. They noted that the prenatal repair group had a reduction in shunt-dependent hydrocephalus and moderate to severe hindbrain herniation but no mortality benefit. Prenatal repair was associated with a higher risk of preterm birth and preterm ruptured membranes, as noted above.

Other risks of prenatal surgery include placental abruption and hysterotomy site dehiscence. In a retrospective study of 237 Brazilian pregnant women undergoing surgery on a fetus with an open spinal defect, preterm labor occurred in 24.2%, premature rupture of membranes in 26.7%, placental abruption in 0.8%, need for a blood transfusion at delivery in 2.1%, and dehiscence at the repair site in 2.5%. Reversal of hindbrain herniation at birth occurred in 71.4% and total operative time was 119 ± 7.6 minutes.

Prenatal surgery in one study was associated with lower Impact on Family Scale scores as well as familial-social impact subscale scores compared to the postnatal surgery group, but no differences on parental stress. Maternal depression scores do not appear to differ by whether prenatal or postnatal surgical closure was conducted for myelomeningocele based on data from the Management of Myelomeningocele Study (detailed below).

Authors of a meta-analysis of 9 studies including 948 pregnancies undergoing prenatal repair of open spina bifida found the following factors significantly reduced the need for postnatal shunt placement: gestational age at surgery <25 weeks (OR 0.3, 95% CI 0.15-0.6; I2=67%) and preoperative lateral ventricle width <15 mm (OR 0.3, 95% CI 0.2-0.4; I2=0.0%).

There was no significant difference in need for intermittent catheterization by 30 months of age between groups enrolled in the Management of Myelomeningocele Study (52% of children in the prenatal surgery group vs. 66% in the postnatal surgery group (relative risk 0.78; 95% CI 0.57-1.07). However, in a later study of 156 children from that trial with a mean age of 7.4 years, fewer children in the prenatal surgery group compared to the postnatal surgery group were undergoing intermittent catheterization (62% vs. 87%). However, there were no differences in rates of augmentation cystoplasty, vesicostomy and urethral dilation between groups.

The incidence of tethered spinal cord may be increased for prenatal vs. postnatal closure of in patients with myelomeningocele based on data from RCTs and controlled cohort studies (overall RR 1.308 (95%CI 1.007 to 1.698, p = .053).

Other studies have also shown that prenatal surgery in normal karyotype newborns can improve social, cognitive, and medical outcomes including reducing the incidence of hydrocephalus and decreasing the severity of Chiari malformations along with better than predicted leg function; however, with significant maternal and fetal risks.
Eighty-five percent of patients with myelomeningocele have shunt-dependent hydrocephalus with the majority requiring shunt placement.
Shunt placement or endoscopic third ventricle (ETV) ventriculostomy are two procedures that are utilized for patients with hydrocephalus.

Based on an analysis of 2985 ETVs performed in 2884 patients of whom 7.6% had myelomeningocele, the overall complication rate following ETV was 8.5% and included permanent morbidity (2.38%), permanent neurological complications such as hemiparesis, gaze palsy, memory disorders, altered consciousness (1.44%), and permanent hormonal morbidity such as diabetes insipidus, weight gain, precocious puberty (0.94%).

Authors of a meta-analysis of 13 studies including 325 patients with myelomeningocele-associated hydrocephalus who underwent endoscopic third ventriculostomy with or without choroid plexus coagulation found that the combined procedure had a significantly higher success rate (75% vs. 48%).

Based on data from Nationwide Inpatient Sample database 1998-2014, of 8233 infants with spina bifida 77.5% had documented hydrocephalus of whom 5876 (71.4%) were treated with ventriculoperitoneal shunt, 331 (4.0%) were treated with ETV, and 2026 (24.6%) remained untreated on initial inpatient stay. Inpatient hydrocephalus treatment failure was higher for patients who received ETV treatment (17.5% ETV failure rate vs. 7.9% VPS failure rate). a meta-analysis of hydrocephalus timing studies revealed no difference between initial inpatient or delayed treatment with respect to shunt failure or infection rates.

In a small case series of 10 fetuses with lumbosacral open spina bifida at a mean gestational age of 27 weeks, endoscopic repair was completed in 8 of 10 fetuses with 1 fetal and 1 neonatal death. One unsuccessful case underwent postnatal repair, 6 of 7 fetuses had complete reversal of hindbrain herniation and 3 babies required ventriculoperitoneal shunting or third ventriculostomy. ACOG 2017 recommended this surgery only be considered within an IRB-approved study.

Open fetal surgery for spina bifida appears to result in lower rates of procedure-related complications than endoscopic surgery based on a meta-analysis of 19 studies. Complications included complete dehiscence (1% vs. 26%, respectively), preterm delivery <34 weeks (80% vs 45%); prelabor rupture of membranes (67% vs 38%), and perinatal death (14% vs 5%). However, data quality was considered low, and the rate of hysterotomy scar complications was high after open surgery

Early spinal cord untethering (in symptomatic patients) can interrupt the progression of NTDs, urologic defects, and limb deformities. Age is the main prognostic factor. Residual neurologic function is more likely to be preserved in the younger patients (less than 2 years old). Monitor for any retethering.
2019 Congress of Neurological Surgeons guidelines recommend surveillance for tethered cord syndrome and inclusion cysts following prenatal repair, based on a systematic review.

In a case series of 14 children with hip instability associated with myelomeningocele, muscle transfer did not add benefit with respect to functional outcomes to periarticular contracture releases and bony procedures alone.
Take an interdisciplinary approach involving various therapies including physical therapy, occupational therapy, educational intervention, and orthotic experts ().
Based on the level of the lesion and the motor and sensory examination, a physical or occupational therapist can create a therapeutic plan to maximize potential for ambulation and minimize deformity.
Orthotics may be required, including wheelchairs, forearm crutches, and braces to stabilize a weight-bearing joint and prevent formation or progression of deformity.
Learning disabilities and motor and cognitive impairments correlate highly with myelomeningocele necessitating educational interventions and speech/occupational/physical therapy.

Cognitive potential can be negatively influenced by hydrocephalus, prematurity, meningitis, shunt infection, and associated congenital anomalies. These patients may require an individualized education plan through the school system.
Patients with myelomeningocele have a higher incidence of low self-esteem, social isolation, and sexual inactivity.
Providers and parents should foster social involvement to minimize associated depression, and treat it if present.
Assess family members for stress, mental health needs and support.

The route of delivery should be individualized. There is no clear evidence for choosing vaginal over cesarean section. Authors of a systematic review and meta-analysis of 9 studies of delivery of 672 infants with open NTDs found no significant difference in motor-anatomic level difference comparing vaginal delivery with Cesarean section; vaginal delivery was associated with fewer rates of shunt requirement and sac disruption (OR 0.37; 95% CI 0.14-0.95 and OR 0.46; 95% CI 0.23-0.90, respectively). There were also no differences in motor-anatomic level difference or ambulation at 2 years between children delivered by prelabor Cesarean compared to those exposed to labor prior to Cesarean delivery.

For fetuses undergoing prenatal myelomeningocele surgical repair, the Canadian 2021 guideline recommends prelabor cesarean delivery performed at 37 weeks at the latest, to prevent possible rupture of the hysterotomy scar during labor.

In utero stem cell application alone or as an adjunct to fetal surgery in animal models with myelomeningocele show promise for improved defect coverage. In an RCT of 40 infants with meningomyelocele undergoing corrective surgery, those randomized to platelet-rich plasma applied over the dura and infused under the skin following closure compared to no application had reduced rates of CSF leakage (one [5%] vs. nine [45%] patients) and partial skin necrosis (15% vs. 65%).

Genetic counseling is recommended. The Canadian 2021 guideline suggests that fetal exome sequencing be considered, but only after multidisciplinary counseling and after appropriate criteria for molecular genetic sequencing are met.
For low level myelomeningocele, clean intermittent catheterization to document residuals, long-term catheterization, and anticholinergic medication may be needed.
In an RCT of 30 children with incontinence due to myelomeningocele, transcutaneous functional electrical stimulation significantly reduced daily incontinence scores.

For children with myelomeningocele and intractable constipation, transcutaneous interferential electrical stimulation may be helpful. Consider assessment for small intestinal bacterial overgrowth in these children, especially with reports of bloating and gas.
Neurologist: for management of associated seizure disorder.
Neurosurgeon: for management of the primary closure of the myelomeningocele defect, hydrocephalus, and spinal cord tethering.
Orthopedic surgery: management of scoliosis and limb deformities.
Urology/nephrology: management of bladder incontinence, poor sphincter tone, vesicoureteral reflux, and progressive renal failure.

This occurs in over 90% of infants with open NTDs; >90% have Arnold–Chiari malformations. Approximately 30% to 40% of infants older than 1 year of age and 70% of children by the age of 10 years will have experienced a shunt malfunction; 2% to 15% of shunt placements and revisions will result in infection of the VP shunt. Most shunt infections occur in the first 1 to 2 months after surgery.

The most common complications associated with shunt placement requiring revision are mechanical obstruction and leakage and shunt infection. One method with increasing usage is endoscopic third ventricle ventriculostomy which has extremely low risk of secondary infection as opposed to a VP shunt.

Measure cranial ventricular dimensions preoperatively when repairing myelomeningocele to determine risk of developing hydrocephalus. This could benefit the surgeon by creating the likelihood of a single stage treatment of spina bifida and hydrocephalus.
Approximately 1 in 5 children with spina bifida have sleep-disordered breathing and another 20% have syringomyelia, while 14% to 29% have underlying seizure disorder.

Over 90% of individuals with myelomeningocele have significant urologic dysfunction, and 20% of these will progress to renal impairment. In a review of 13 retrospective studies, total continence was reported in 449/1192 (37.7%; range 8%-85%) of adult patients with spina bifida; associated risk factors for incontinence were neurological level of the lesion and hydrocephalus. Renal function was impaired to some degree in 290/1128 (25.7%; range 3.0%-81.8%) but end-stage renal disease was seen in only 12/958 (1.3%).

Based on data from the National Spina Bifida Patient Registry 2009 through 2015, of 5250 patients with a mean age of 16.6 years, 92.6% used some form of bladder management, 45.8% reported bladder continence, and 22.4% had undergone bladder continence surgery. Among the 1,372 adults, 45.8% did not take medication for incontinence but 76.8% performed intermittent catheterization.

Intradetrusor injection of botulinum toxin A may be effective in children with myelomeningocele who have neurogenic detrusor overactivity. In a case series of 53 children with spina bifida, clinical improvement occurred in 66% patients; however, urodynamic outcomes were poor resulting in a global success rate of only 30%. At 3.7 years, 23 patients (43.4%) required augmentation cystoplasty.

Hip subluxation/dislocation is present in 35% to 50% of children and 75% have foot deformities. Approximately 90% of children with lesions T12 or higher will have scoliosis. Pathologic bone fractures are developed in 10% to 30% of children. Risk factors for fractures in children with spina bifida include higher levels of neurological involvement, non-ambulatory status, physical inactivity, hypercalciuria, higher body fat levels, contractures, and a previous spontaneous fracture.
Risk of recurrence in a woman with a previous child with an NTD is about 2% to 3%. B The adjusted OR of a family history of NTD for spina bifida is 6.99 (95% CI 3.87-12.6).
Walking ability predicts independence; 65% walk with L4 to S1 defect, 20% with L1 to L3, and 0% with T12 level or above. B
Worse cognitive outcomes are associated with the presence of seizures, number of shunt revisions, higher level lesions, history of CNS infection, and oculomotor findings. B
Most patients will present with long-term evolutional problems with regards to their neurologic, orthopedic, and urologic systems.

Many patients with myelomeningocele will develop scoliosis up to the age of 15 years until the adolescent growth spurt is complete. See for risk factors for scoliosis in patients with myelomeningocele.
Type I Chiari malformations are found in 0.9% of asymptomatic adults on MRI.
See for poor prognostic indicators in patients with myelomeningeocele.

Among 5165 infants with spina bifida born during 1979 to 2003 (from 10 birth defects registries in the United States), 1-year survival improved for all races; for whites from 88% to 96%, blacks from 79% to 88%, and Hispanics from 88% to 93%). Racial disparity in mortality was noted for Hispanics vs. whites among infants of low birth weight (4- to 6-fold difference) and for black vs. white infants of normal birth weight.
Early untethering can interrupt the progression of neurologic deficits, urologic dysfunction, and limb deformities.
Nearly all patients with repaired myelomeningocele develop Arnold–Chiari malformation; 20% of these patients have clinical signs of decreased brain function.
An IQ of 85 is the cutoff point between dependence and independence. Early detection allows families to plan for the future; 45% to 55% of patients with myelomeningocele live independently.
Impaired executive function reveals deficits in working memory, problem solving, focused attention (mainly inattentive type), and higher order planning.
Another predictor of independence is walking ability. Walking ability is as follows: 65%—L4 to S1 defect, 20%—L1 to L3, and 0%—T12 level or above.

In a 10-year follow-up of 42 of 54 patients who underwent fetal myelomeningocele surgery at one institution, 33 (79%) were community ambulators, 3 (9%) were household ambulators, and 6 (14%) are wheelchair dependent. Normal bladder function was reported in 26%. Abnormalities of behavioral adaptive skills appear to be more common than impairment in executive function, and need for shunting was associated with significant impairment in the former.
Worse cognitive outcomes were directly related to the presence of seizures, number of shunt revisions, higher level lesions, a history of CNS infection, and oculomotor findings.

Follow-up studies of most of children enrolled in the Management of Myelomeningocele Study showed reduced hindbrain herniation and need for shunt diversion at 12 months in those randomized to prenatal surgery.

Thirty-month follow-up on 183 infants from the Management of Myelomeningocele Study, demonstrated that those randomized to prenatal repair had a higher composite score of mental development and motor function (199.4 ± 80.5 vs. 166.7 ± 76.7), with a higher percentage achieving independent ambulation (44.8% vs. 23.9%), higher WeeFIM self-care scores (20.8 vs. 19.0), higher functional level of at least 2 better than anatomic level (26.4% vs. 11.4%), and higher mean Bayley Scales of Infant Development psychomotor development index (17.3% vs. 15.1%). There was no difference in cognitive development.
Better motor function was also documented at a mean of 7.4 years.

At the most recent follow-up of 161 children at ages 5.9-10.3 years, there was no significant difference between prenatal and postnatal surgery groups in overall adaptive behavior or improved cognitive ability, but those in the prenatal surgery group had improved mobility and independent functioning as evidenced by walking without orthotics or assistive devices more often (29% vs 11%, respectively) and fewer had surgeries for shunt placement and revision (47% vs 70%, respectively).
Monitor for development or progression of hydrocephalus after primary closure of myelomeningocele.
Carefully assess visual function and stability including evolution of refractive errors and strabismus.
Monitor for development of scoliosis.
Monitor for any neurological deterioration such as pain, weakness, urinary symptoms, and sensory changes requiring immediate untethering of the spinal cord to minimize neurodeficits.
Follow bone mineral density in patients with myelomeningocele as they are at risk for pathologic bone fractures.
Periconceptual folate supplementation provides a significant protective effect against NTDs. Educate women regarding reducing the risk of NTDs periconceptually and about folate supplementation.
Monitor families for increased levels of parental psychological stress which can contribute to maladjustment of children with myelomeningocele.

feature.caption: Roles of Team Members for the Patient with Myelomeningocele or Other Serious Neural Tube Defect.

list.listitem: Refer to appropriate subspecialists.
Coordinate physical and occupational therapy.
Monitor for cognitive deficits. If present, refer for early intervention and educational testing.
Monitor for signs of depression, social isolation, and low self-esteem.
Follow growth parameters closely.
Monitor for hydrocephalus and any other neurologic changes that may suggest a tethered cord.
Refer for specific orthotic needs such as wheelchairs, forearm crutches, and braces.
Coordinate therapies and subspecialty appointments.
Monitor family for psychosocial stress and counseling needs.

Inform parents of the IDEA (Individuals with Disabilities Education Act) and Section 504 of the Rehabilitation Act to ensure that their child's educational needs are being reasonably accommodated in the school and classroom environment.
Based on the level of the lesion and motor/sensory involvement, devise a therapeutic program that will maximize the patient's ambulation potential.
Teach the patient and his/her family lifetime skills that will help the patient achieve independence (cooking, cleaning, bathing, dressing, etc).
Maximize the patient's ambulation by instructing the patient how to utilize his/her orthotics most effectively.
Monitor growth parameters.
Adjust dietary calories to maintain a healthy weight.
With the higher incidence of pathologic fractures, ensure that the patient is receiving adequate amounts of vitamin D and calcium.
Provide early surgical intervention for closure of the primary back defect.
Monitor for hydrocephalus. If present, shunt placement is recommended.
Monitor for shunt malfunction, shunt infection, Chiari II malformation, tethered cord, syringomyelia, chronic headaches, and seizures.
Assess the level of spinal cord dysfunction to plan more specifically for orthopedic management.
Monitor for foot deformities, subluxation/dislocation of the hips, knee contractures, scoliosis, kyphosis, and pathologic fractures.
Monitor for orthotic needs to maximize ambulation.
Manage neurogenic bladder.
Prevent and monitor for UTIs.
Monitor for presence of vesicoureteral reflux.
Preserve renal function.
Manage urine incontinence with the ultimate goal of achieving social continence.
Manage bowel incontinence.
Avoid chronic constipation and impaction.
Achieve an effective bowel continence program.

feature.caption: Risk Factors for Scoliosis (J Bone Joint Surg 2002;84A:1389-1394).

list.listitem: Higher clinical motor level, especially with thoracic/upper lumbar lesions
Spinal cord tethering
Lower extremity spasticity
Higher the last intact laminar arch estimated via x-ray at 3-6 y of age
Nonambulators
Higher level lesions increase the risk of complications
Presence of hydrocephalus
Underlying seizures
Number of shunt revisions
Spinal cord tethering
History of CNS infections
